title: Candied violets
subtitle: fresh violet flowers preserved in a sugar syrup coating and dried until firm
excerpt: Candied violets are fresh edible violet flowers coated in a light sugar syrup and dried until the coating is firm and crystalline. They are used to decorate cakes, chocolates, and petits fours. The process is gentle and slow: the flowers are dipped in syrup, lifted out carefully, and left to dry in a single layer on baking paper.
sourceNotes: Candied violets have been produced in Toulouse, France, since at least the nineteenth century, where the Violette de Toulouse became a regional speciality. They appear in English and French confectionery books throughout the Victorian and Edwardian periods as a decoration for cakes and desserts.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 months.

content.text: Candied violets are fresh flowers coated in a thin sugar syrup shell and dried until the coating is hard and slightly translucent. They take 24 to 48 hours to dry fully, but most of that is hands-off time. Use only edible violet species such as Viola odorata or Viola tricolor. The flowers must be picked fresh and used the same day.

Put the 150 g of caster sugar and water in a small saucepan. Heat over low heat, stirring until the sugar has dissolved. Bring to the boil and cook for 2 minutes. Remove from the heat and leave to cool to a temperature comfortable to work with, about 10 minutes. The syrup should still be warm and fluid.
Spread the extra fine sugar in a shallow dish. Line a cooling rack with baking paper.
Hold a violet by its short stem. Using a small pastry brush, paint the warm syrup over every petal surface, front and back. The coating should be thin and even.
Hold the coated flower over the dish of fine sugar and spoon it gently over the petals, turning to coat all sides. Shake off any excess and place on the rack. Repeat with all flowers.
Leave to dry at room temperature for 24 to 48 hours, away from damp or draughts. The flowers are ready when the coating feels completely firm and dry to the touch.
Store in a single layer in an airtight container between sheets of baking paper. They keep for up to 3 months at room temperature.

attrs.problem: Flowers losing their shape and petals drooping during drying
attrs.avoid: Avoid too thick a syrup coating; heavy syrup weighs the petals down.
attrs.fix: Apply a very thin, even coat of syrup and remove all excess before sugaring. Prop any drooping petals into position with a small fold of paper while they dry.

attrs.problem: Sugar coating soft or sticky after drying
attrs.avoid: Avoid high humidity; moisture in the air prevents the coating from setting firm.
attrs.fix: Dry in the warmest, driest spot available. An oven left on its lowest setting with the door slightly open works well if the kitchen is damp.
